_areas_note: One peak, one road: Lincoln Peak is approached from the Middle Fork Nooksack road (FS 38), not from anywhere on Mount Baker's north or south sides. VERIFIED AS BELONGING HERE. Both routes on the peak start from this road. The X Couloir on the southwest face is the standard line and is reached by walking the road up its switchbacks to about the seventh, then taking an old path and scrambling north into the Rankin Creek basin, over a saddle near 5,480 ft and out onto the ridge above Wallace Creek. The north ridge is approached from the same ground, continuing up the basin toward the snowfield west of the Black Buttes and the Thunder Glacier side. DO NOT GIVE THIS PEAK HELIOTROPE RIDGE OR SCHRIEBERS MEADOW CAMPS. Both of those serve Mount Baker itself and its immediate satellites from the opposite side of the mountain, and neither reaches Lincoln without crossing the volcano. The Rankin Creek approach exists precisely because it is shorter than trying to come around from Heliotrope, and it avoids that trailhead's crowds. ROAD STATUS DOMINATES THE PLANNING HERE — the Middle Fork Nooksack road washed out in the December 2025 storms and has been barriered at milepost 7 since, with no repair timeline announced as of mid-2026. The Rankin Creek switchbacks begin around milepost 12.5, so at present a party adds five and a half road miles each way on top of an already long approach. Verify the road before committing; in past seasons a gate near milepost 9.9 was the limit early in the year, an ordinary car could reach the second or third switchback around 2,650 to 2,780 ft, and a high-clearance vehicle sometimes made the fifth near 3,420 ft.

sites.name: Wallace Creek basin ridge camp
sites.capacity: Two or three tents on the last flat ground beside the highest trees; more parties than that and people are pitching on open snow
sites.water: Running water is unreliable at this height. In spring, when the peak is in condition, you melt snow, which is what nearly every party does. Later in the year expect to carry from the tarns at the saddle below
sites.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, whose boundary you cross on the way up into the basin. No overnight wilderness permit is required and none is issued for this area. Party size is capped at twelve. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass covers parking at the road end. This is national forest, not national park, so no park backcountry permit applies and none can be obtained for it. Stoves rather than fires, and pack out everything including waste on snow
sites.notes: This is the established high camp for Lincoln and the one nearly every ascent uses. It sits on the ridge overlooking the Wallace Creek basin, right at the last stand of trees, with the Black Buttes and the summit block in view above. Reaching it means walking the road to about the seventh switchback, picking up the old track that leads toward Rankin Creek, scrambling into the basin, passing east Rankin Lake, then climbing mellow snow north to the saddle near 5,480 ft and east up the basin below Seward to the ridge. From here the X Couloir on the southwest face and the north ridge are both single-push summit days, and both are long, steep, exposed snow and ice, which is why the camp is high. The peak is in condition in spring, when fresh snow has mostly stopped falling but nights are still cold enough to hold the snow, ice and rock together; by high summer the face becomes loose and dangerous. Expect the trees to be buried and the ground to be snow. Nothing here is sheltered from weather coming off Baker.

sites.name: East Rankin Lake
sites.capacity: Two or three tents around the lake basin on snow or, late in the year, on gravel and heather away from the shore
sites.water: The lake, once it has melted out. In the spring climbing season it is frozen and buried, so plan on melting snow
sites.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass for the vehicle at the road end. No campfires above treeline; use a stove. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and keep off the heather when it is out
sites.notes: The lower of the two natural stopping places on the approach, in the Rankin Creek basin below the saddle. It is the sensible camp for a party that started late, that is walking extra road miles because of the washout, or that wants an easier carry on day one and a longer summit day on day two. From here the route continues north on easy-angled snow to the small saddle and then east into the upper basin, so nothing is wasted. The cost is close to a thousand feet of climbing left over for summit morning on a route where the difficulties start high. In spring the lake is a flat white plain and easy to camp on; later in the season the basin brushes up and the ground around the water is soggy.

sites.name: Saddle tarns above Rankin Creek
sites.capacity: One or two tents on the flats beside the small lakes; informal ground with no established site
sites.water: Two small tarns sit right at the saddle. They are usually still under snow through the spring climbing season, so treat them as a summer source and otherwise melt snow
sites.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit, twelve-person limit, recreation pass at the road end. Stove only
sites.notes: The small saddle north of the Rankin basin, with a pair of tarns beside it, sitting between east Rankin Lake and the climb east into the upper basin below Seward. It is a stopgap rather than a destination: only a few hundred feet above the lake and still well short of the ridge camp, so it is chosen mostly by parties caught by weather or darkness on the way up. It is a windy notch, which is worth knowing before you commit to it in a storm. The one thing it does well is mark the point where the approach turns from valley travel to open alpine snow, so it is a useful place to re-assess conditions before carrying a heavy load higher.

sites.name: Middle Fork Nooksack road switchbacks
sites.capacity: Roadside pullouts at the lower switchbacks take a couple of vehicles each; there are no built sites, no tables and no toilets
sites.water: Creeks cross and run down the road in spring, and Rankin Creek is nearby. Treat anything you take
sites.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, outside the wilderness boundary at this elevation. Dispersed roadside camping, no permit, no reservation. Check the current fire restrictions before lighting anything and expect fires to be banned outright in dry spells; a stove is the safe assumption. Pack out all rubbish
sites.notes: Sleeping at the vehicle the night before is the normal way to start this climb, because the approach is long and parties want to be walking in the dark. The switchbacks above the road's lower section give rough pullouts around 2,650 to 3,420 ft depending on how far the surface lets you drive; past the first switchback the brush closes in and the potholes get serious, and a small car will not make it far. With the road currently barriered at milepost 7 the practical bivouac is wherever the closure puts you, and the Rankin Creek switchbacks are then a long walk or bike ride away — a bicycle to the closure point is worth considering. No elevation is given here because the usable spot depends entirely on how far up the road is open in a given season, which changes.
